dimensions.summary: The money-path engineering here is unusually deliberate for a largely non-engineer-built repo: every stage appends output before marking its checkpoint, parallel_map's contract (in-order yield, main-thread writes, exception surfaces after yielded items are safe) is real — I verified against CPython's Executor.map that all tasks are submitted eagerly but the result iterator's finally-clause cancels unstarted futures on early exit, so an exception wastes at most the in-flight worker calls — and the DAD steps 2–3 and pref pipeline are exemplary: stop_reason guards with skip-without-checkpoint retry semantics, plus belt-and-braces done-detection that consults both the checkpoint and the output file, making them robust even to a lost checkpoint. Cost logging is sound on both backends (thread-safe append, per-run log path, notional-cost fallback for claude_code, loud unknown-model pricing warning, attempt/duration tags); the "cost this session" label actually reports whole-run cumulative cost on resume, a cosmetic nit. The defects cluster in two places. First, the older SDF layers lag the DAD standard: no layer checks stop_reason, and layer 4 — the alignment-critical rewrite — fails open on truncation by silently checkpointing the un-rewritten draft into the corpus, exactly the failure DAD step 3 was built to prevent. Second, the persistence primitives themselves are not crash-safe: Checkpoint rewrites its JSON in place (a kill mid-write bricks --resume) and load_jsonl tolerates no partial trailing line, so the recovery path for the most common failure (interrupted run) can itself corrupt, and layers 2–4's checkpoint-only done-detection turns that into re-billing plus duplicate records. DAD step 1c is the one stage that violates the repo's own write-per-item contract, deferring all persistence to the end of a batch. The flagged ruff seeds (B023, B905) are all verified benign as written. Fixes are mostly small and can copy patterns that already exist elsewhere in the same codebase.

findings.title: SDF layer 4 (alignment-critical rewrite) fails open on truncation: un-rewritten draft is checkpointed into the corpus and never retried
findings.evidence: Line 43-49: `api.call_claude(...)` is invoked WITHOUT `return_stop_reason=True` (max_tokens=6000). Lines 52-61: if `<improved_document>` tags are absent — which is exactly what a max_tokens truncation or a refusal produces — the fallback sets `rewritten = draft["content"]` with only a note in `review_notes` ("Parse error — no <improved_document> tags; kept original draft."), no runtime print. Line 80: the record is then `checkpoint.mark_done(record["doc_id"])`, so --resume never retries it. Contrast dad_pipeline/step3_rewrite.py:58-89, which checks stop_reason, retries once at 8000 tokens, and refuses to checkpoint a truncated rewrite. CLAUDE.md calls layer 4 "the quality-critical call" (TCW ablation: 19x on misalignment rate).
findings.failure_scenario: A long layer-3 draft (e.g. the single-doc fallback path can consume most of layer 3's 6000-token budget) needs review notes + full rewrite > 6000 output tokens. stop_reason=max_tokens, the closing tag never arrives, the original un-rewritten draft is silently kept, marked done, scored at layer 5 (drafts routinely score >=7), and enters sdf_corpus.jsonl having skipped the pipeline's alignment-critical transform. Nothing in the final record or console reveals it; the only trace is review_notes in an intermediate file nobody gates on.
findings.recommendation: Mirror step3_rewrite.py: call with `return_stop_reason=True`; on stop_reason=="max_tokens" retry once at a doubled cap; if still truncated or the tags are missing, print, log to a rewrite_failures.jsonl, and `continue` WITHOUT mark_done so --resume retries. The keep-original fallback should survive only for genuinely well-terminated responses that omitted tags, and even then emit a console warning. Update the pinned test at tests/test_sdf_layers.py:165 deliberately (per CLAUDE.md's flip-the-test-deliberately rule).

findings.title: Checkpoint and JSONL persistence are not crash-safe: a kill mid-write bricks --resume, and the likely operator recovery re-bills a whole stage
findings.evidence: Checkpoint.mark_done (lines 296-304) rewrites the entire checkpoint file in place: `with open(self.path, "w") ...: json.dump(...)` — no temp-file + os.replace. Checkpoint.__init__ (lines 288-291) does a bare `json.load` with no error handling, so a truncated file raises JSONDecodeError at stage start. load_jsonl (lines 60-65) likewise raises on a partial trailing line, which is what a crash mid-`append_jsonl` (lines 48-52, multi-KB document records, no single-write guarantee) leaves behind.
findings.failure_scenario: A $50 run is killed (Ctrl-C, OOM, power loss) during one of the thousands of mark_done rewrites or mid-append of a document record. The next `--resume` crashes with a JSONDecodeError traceback before making any API call. A non-engineer contributor's natural fix — delete `_checkpoint.json` (or the .jsonl) — re-bills every item in that stage, and in layers 2-4 (which trust only the checkpoint, see separate finding) additionally appends duplicate records alongside the survivors.
findings.recommendation: In mark_done, write to `self.path.with_suffix('.json.tmp')` then `os.replace` (atomic on POSIX and Windows). In __init__, catch (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError), warn to stderr, and start from an empty completed-set — safe because every stage writes output before marking, and the output-file cross-check pattern (layer 5 / steps 2-3 / pref) makes recovery free. In load_jsonl, tolerate exactly one malformed FINAL line with a stderr warning (still raise on malformed interior lines). Add tests for all three per the checkpoint/resume money-path test rule.
instances: shared/utils.py:60-65 (load_jsonl intolerant of partial trailing line)

findings.title: DAD step 1c defers all persistence to end-of-batch: one refine failure discards the whole batch's paid 1b + 1c work
findings.evidence: The 1c fan-out (lines 756-769) collects results only into the in-memory `refined_by_pid`; record assembly and every `utils.append_jsonl(record, output_path)` happen in a separate loop afterwards (lines 771-815). This is the one stage that violates the parallel_map contract's intent ("items already yielded are safely checkpointed", shared/utils.py:17-25) — yielded refine results are NOT persisted until the entire batch's zip loop finishes.
findings.failure_scenario: On the claude_code backend, the subscription window is exhausted (UsageLimitExceeded, deliberately not retried — shared/api.py:85-91) at refine 9 of 10. The exception propagates out of the zip at line 767; the record loop never runs; nothing from the batch reaches dilemmas.jsonl. --resume finds all 10 scenarios unfilled and re-bills the 16k-token 1b batch call (line 729) plus all 10 Sonnet refine calls — including the 8 that already succeeded. Same loss for an API-backend refine that exhausts its 8 tenacity retries.
findings.recommendation: Merge the two loops: iterate `zip(batch-with-drafts, parallel_map(_refine, ...))` and, per item, assemble the record (ID assignment stays main-thread, input-order) and append it to output_path immediately — matching layers 2-5. Alternatively, append each refine result to refinements.jsonl inside the zip loop and consult it before re-calling on retry. Add the resume test asserting zero API calls for scenarios whose refines completed.

findings.title: Layers 2-4 trust only the checkpoint for done-ness: a crash in the append-to-mark window duplicates records (and documents) on resume
findings.evidence: layer4_rewrite.py:30 computes `pending = [d for d in drafts if not checkpoint.is_done(d["doc_id"])]` without consulting the already-loaded `existing` rewrites (line 27-28); the append (line 79) precedes mark_done (line 80). Layers 2 and 3 have the same shape with a wider window — a whole type/subtype's records are appended (layer2:117-119, layer3:182-184) before the single mark (120, 185). Contrast layer5_score.py:58-61, step2_responses.py:110-121, step3_rewrite.py:41-45, and pref_pipeline/run.py:129-140, which all cross-check the output file.
findings.failure_scenario: Run killed between layer 4's append and mark_done for doc X. --resume re-bills X's rewrite and appends a second record with the same doc_id; layer 5 receives both (run.py loads rewrites.jsonl), scores both (one extra paid call), and two independent temperature-1.0 rewrites of the same draft can both pass threshold and land in sdf_corpus.jsonl (the 0.90 shingle cull is not guaranteed to catch them). In layer 2 the resume regenerates the whole type next to surviving partial records, yielding colliding subtype_ids ("5_0" twice) that layer 3 then drafts twice — duplicate cost and near-duplicate corpus content.
findings.recommendation: Layer 4: one line — exclude doc_ids present in `existing` from pending, exactly like layer 5. Layers 2/3: on load, dedupe existing records by subtype_id/doc_id (keep first) and treat a type/subtype as done if its records exist on disk, or write each type's records via a single save-then-mark sequence. The atomic-checkpoint fix (separate finding) shrinks but does not close this window.

findings.title: Pref pipeline re-reads the live prompts file on --resume: an edited file silently mispairs arm responses across different prompts
findings.evidence: Arms are frozen into the run (`inputs/arm_prompts.yaml`, lines 111-119) precisely so resume replays them, but the prompts themselves are re-loaded from the live `--prompts`/config path every invocation (lines 94-101). The per-arm cache is keyed only by (pair_id, arm) (lines 130-131, 146-148), and pair_id derives from prompt_id alone (line 139), not from the prompt text. Separately, line 39 reads only `user_message`/`prompt`, while the CLI help on line 80 and CLAUDE.md both promise a `refined` field.
findings.failure_scenario: Arm a succeeds for pair_AW-0007, arm b fails (pair deferred, per lines 159-171). The contributor tweaks the prompt wording in the JSONL (or regenerates dilemmas.jsonl), then --resume: arm a's cached response to the OLD text (line 146-148) is paired with arm b's fresh response to the NEW text and recorded under the new user_message (lines 179-188). Raters blind-compare responses to two different prompts, and the resulting preferences.jsonl — potential DPO data — is silently wrong. The `refined`-field gap is loud but confusing: a refined-only JSONL exits with "No usable prompts" despite matching the documented contract.
findings.recommendation: Freeze the prompt set like the arms: on run creation copy the resolved prompts to `run_dir/inputs/prompts.jsonl` and load from there on --resume (warn if --prompts is also passed and differs). Cheaper stopgap: store a hash of user_message in each arm_responses.jsonl row and refuse the cached response when it mismatches. Also add `r.get("refined")` to the fallback chain in _load_prompts (line 39) to honor the documented contract.

findings.title: SDF layer 3 never checks stop_reason: truncated draft batches silently shrink the corpus and can admit a sentence-trimmed fragment
findings.evidence: Lines 143-146: call_claude at max_tokens=6000 without `return_stop_reason` while requesting `count` documents in one response. Lines 154-159: only complete `<document>...</document>` blocks are kept, so a max_tokens cutoff silently drops the trailing document(s). Lines 161-164: when NO complete block exists, the whole truncated output is trimmed "back to the last complete sentence" and becomes a draft. Line 185 marks the subtype done regardless of how many of `count` docs materialized. (Layers 1-2 also skip stop_reason but fail safe: utils.extract_json's broken-container logic, shared/utils.py:101-110, raises on truncated arrays rather than salvaging fragments.)
findings.failure_scenario: documents_per_subtype=3 with verbose drafts: the third document is cut mid-paragraph, silently dropped, and the subtype is checkpointed done with 2 docs — the corpus undershoots its configured size with no signal beyond a per-subtype count print. Worse, a single-document response truncated before its closing tag becomes a fragment ending at an arbitrary sentence — grammatical but incomplete (an argument that stops halfway) — which layer 4 rewrites and layer 5 can score >=7 into the training corpus.
findings.recommendation: Use `return_stop_reason=True`; on stop_reason=="max_tokens" either retry once with a raised cap (step3_rewrite.py:65-70 pattern) or accept the complete tagged docs but print a loud per-subtype shortfall warning and record `requested`/`delivered` in the checkpoint record; never take the untagged-fallback path (line 161-164) for a max_tokens response — skip without mark_done so --resume retries.
instances: sdf_pipeline/layer1_document_types.py:41 and sdf_pipeline/layer2_subtypes.py:57 (no stop_reason, but fail-safe via extract_json)

findings.title: --resume applies the live config's models/knobs silently; only a backend change is warned about
findings.evidence: warn_if_backend_changed (lines 254-279) compares only the `backend` key of run_manifest.json against the live config. Both orchestrators call `api.init(args.config, ...)` and pass the freshly loaded config to every stage (sdf_pipeline/run.py:32,60; dad_pipeline/run.py:40,68), so per-stage model overrides, max_tokens, thresholds, and worker counts all follow the live config.yaml on resume while the manifest still records the originals.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor edits config.yaml between sessions (e.g. flips draft_model from haiku to sonnet to test, forgets to revert) then resumes a full-scale run: the remaining half of layer 3 runs at 3x the intended price, mixed-model within one stage, and the run_manifest.json snapshot now misdescribes what actually generated the corpus — undermining the manifest's reproducibility promise. No warning is emitted.
findings.recommendation: Extend warn_if_backend_changed into warn_if_config_changed: diff the manifest's config against the live one for the money-relevant keys (`model`, `sdf.*_model`, `dad.*_model`, `max_tokens`, `temperature`, scale knobs) and print each drift on --resume. Optionally offer resuming FROM the manifest config as the default, with the live config opt-in.

findings.title: Layer 5 parse-failure fallback fabricates scores of 5 — fails closed only while min_score_threshold stays above 5; non-dict JSON crashes the stage
findings.evidence: Lines 79-82: a JSONDecodeError from the scoring call is replaced by `{"alignment": 5, "realism": 5, "diversity": 5, "notes": "Parse error."}`. That is below the shipped threshold (config.yaml:13, min_score_threshold: 7) purely by coincidence of configuration; nothing pins the invariant. Also lines 93-96 call `scores.get(...)` — if extract_json returns a JSON array (a plausible model slip), AttributeError crashes the whole layer mid-run, discarding in-flight paid calls.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor lowers min_score_threshold to 5 for a cheap dev run (the natural knob to loosen) and keeps the output: every scoring response that fails to parse now passes BOTH gates with fabricated scores, putting unscored documents into the training corpus with only a "Parse error." note buried in scores.jsonl. Separately, one array-shaped scoring response crashes layer 5 and wastes up to `workers` in-flight scoring calls.
findings.recommendation: Make the fallback structurally fail-closed: use scores of 0 (or a `parse_error: true` flag that the pass-filter at lines 118-121 rejects explicitly) instead of a value that happens to sit below today's threshold; wrap the parse in `if not isinstance(scores, dict): scores = {}` before the .get calls. One-line test each.

findings.title: Ruff seeds verified: B023 loop-variable capture at layer2:114 and all four B905 zips are benign as written (fragile, not buggy)
findings.evidence: The lambda at line 114 captures `note` by reference, but is safe: `zip(wave, parallel_map(...))` (line 113) fully consumes the generator within the same wave iteration — Executor.map (verified in CPython source) submits ALL of the wave's tasks at the first pull, while `note` still holds that wave's value, and `note` is only reassigned (line 112) after zip exhausts `wave`. B905: layer2:113, layer3_draft.py:180, and step1_dilemmas.py:767 each zip a list against `parallel_map` over that same list (equal length by construction; a worker exception propagates through zip rather than mispairing); diversity.py:152 zips chunk indices against embed_texts output, which returns exactly one row per input (shared/embeddings.py:134-167).
findings.failure_scenario: No current failure. The maintenance risk: the `note` capture silently becomes a real cross-wave bug if anyone breaks the consume-within-iteration pattern (e.g. collecting the generators first, filtering the zip, or adding an early `break`), and the strict-less zips would silently drop items if parallel_map ever gained an error-skipping mode. In a repo maintained by non-engineers via automated review, these are the kind of latent traps that survive refactors.
findings.recommendation: Bind the wave note at definition time — `lambda dt, note=note: generate_subtypes(dt, note)` — and add `strict=True` to the four zips (free at these sizes; also promptly closes parallel_map's ThreadPoolExecutor by exhausting the generator). Pure hardening; no behavior change expected, existing tests should pass unmodified.

dimensions.summary: The repo has seven distinct LLM-output parsing implementations spread across six files: shared/utils.extract_json (longest-complete-value, fail-closed on broken containers, well-tested — the only shared one, used by SDF layers 1/2/5); dad_pipeline/step1_dilemmas.py's trio (_parse_json_array / _parse_json_object / _salvage_objects — fence-strip, bracket-slice, then a hand-rolled brace-matching state machine that salvages complete objects out of truncated arrays); dad_pipeline/step2_responses._parse_scope (fence-strip + greedy brace-slice, strict=False, returns {}); evals/audit_sdf._parse_json_block (fence-strip + first-bracket raw_decode, raises); inline fence-strip + bare json.loads in evals/score_sdf.py and score_dad.py (placeholder scores on failure); and regex tag extraction with degrading fallbacks in sdf layers 3/4. These embody three conflicting salvage philosophies — extract_json deliberately REJECTS fragments of broken containers (documented, tested), step 1b deliberately HARVESTS fragments because its re-request loop makes partial results safe, and the score/audit sites want whole-or-nothing with silent degradation — and one hard-won lesson (strict=False for temperature-1 prose JSON, encoded in _parse_scope with a test citing "the historical cause of silently empty scopes") that never propagated to the five sibling parsers. The worst concrete defects: SDF layer 5 checkpoints parse failures with placeholder scores, permanently discarding paid layer-3+4 work with no resume retry; and the step-1 parsers' strict decoding re-bills 16k-token batch calls for rescuable output. Consolidation is very tractable: extract_json's algorithm subsumes every whole-value site unchanged if it gains strict=False and an expect="array"/"object" parameter, and _salvage_objects should move to shared/utils as the single documented truncated-batch variant; only step 1b legitimately needs it. Test coverage is inverted relative to risk — extract_json is thoroughly tested while the most intricate parser (_salvage_objects, coverage lines 544–568) and both eval scorers (0%) have none.

findings.title: Layer 5 checkpoints score-parse failures, permanently discarding paid layer-3/4 documents with no resume retry
findings.evidence: Lines 79-82: `try: scores = utils.extract_json(raw) except json.JSONDecodeError: scores = {"alignment": 5, "realism": 5, "diversity": 5, "notes": "Parse error."}`. The record is then appended to scores.jsonl and `checkpoint.mark_done(record["doc_id"])` (line 115), so on --resume the doc sits in existing_scores and is never re-scored. With the default `min_score_threshold: 7` (config.yaml line 13), placeholder 5s fail the filter at lines 118-121 and the doc is dropped from the corpus. No stop_reason check on the scoring call (lines 73-78) either.
findings.failure_scenario: The scoring model puts a literal newline inside the `notes` string (the exact temperature-1 failure step2's tests document as 'the historical cause of silently empty scopes') or wraps the object in prose that breaks all candidates. extract_json raises, the doc gets 5/5/5, is checkpointed, and silently vanishes from the final corpus. The layer-3 draft and the expensive layer-4 constitution rewrite for that doc — the two paid quality-critical calls — are permanently lost; --resume retries nothing because the checkpoint says done. If a contributor later lowers min_score_threshold to 5 for a dev run, the same path instead inserts docs with fabricated scores into the corpus.
findings.recommendation: Match the DAD step-2/3 contract that CLAUDE.md advertises ('failed work is not checkpointed, so --resume retries it'): on JSONDecodeError return a sentinel from score_document, and on the main thread log it to a score_failures.jsonl and skip both append_jsonl and mark_done so --resume retries the scoring call (the draft/rewrite are already checkpointed, so the retry costs one cheap scoring call). Also request return_stop_reason=True and treat stop_reason=='max_tokens' as a failed attempt, and validate `isinstance(scores, dict)` before .get (a list-wrapped judge response currently raises AttributeError past the except and kills the layer).
instances: sdf_pipeline/layer5_score.py:111-115 (failure record appended + checkpointed like a success)
findings.verifier_notes: All cited lines match current code: layer5_score.py:79-82 substitutes 5/5/5 placeholder scores on json.JSONDecodeError, lines 111-115 append and checkpoint that record like a success, lines 55-61 make --resume reuse it without re-scoring, and lines 118-121 with min_score_threshold: 7 (config.yaml:13) drop the doc from the final corpus. Executed utils.extract_json against a scores object with a literal newline inside the notes string and against prose-wrapped truncated JSON — both raise, and tests/test_dad_steps.py:211-214 confirms the newline case as the documented historical failure step 2 fixed but layer 5 did not. The scoring call omits return_stop_reason and api.call_claude only warns (api.py:484-489), so max_tokens truncation feeds the same path; the low-threshold variant (fabricated scores entering the corpus) also holds. Minor nuance only: the failure is discoverable in scores.jsonl ("notes": "Parse error.") and the rewritten text survives in layer-4 output, but no automated retry exists — consistent with the finding as stated.

findings.title: Strict JSON decoding in step-1 parsers and extract_json rejects control-character payloads that step 2 already learned to accept, re-billing 16k-token batch calls
findings.evidence: step2_responses.py:46 uses `json.loads(text.strip(), strict=False)` with the comment 'strict=False accepts literal newlines/tabs inside string values — the way a prose-heavy JSON object at temperature 1.0 most often goes invalid', and tests/test_dad_steps.py:210-214 calls this 'the historical cause of silently empty scopes'. But step1's parsers use strict defaults: json.loads at step1_dilemmas.py:564 (_salvage_objects), :578 and :584 (_parse_json_array), :600 (_parse_json_object); and shared/utils.py:90 builds `json.JSONDecoder()` with strict=True for extract_json.
findings.failure_scenario: A 1b batch response (max_tokens=16000, step1_dilemmas.py:729) contains multi-paragraph dilemma prompts where the model emits a literal newline inside a JSON string — the repo's own documented most-common temperature-1 failure. Whole-text parse fails, bracket-slice fails, and _salvage_objects' per-object json.loads also fails on the same control character, so structurally intact objects are dropped. Affected scenarios are re-requested in a fresh 16k-token batch call that is just as likely to fail the same way; the loop burns up to max_calls (8x the batch count, line 703) or exits via the 3-consecutive-failures SystemExit (line 744), billing thousands of wasted tokens. In 1c, the same defect silently discards the paid refine call and keeps the unrefined 1b draft (line 787). At layers 1/2/5 it converts usable responses into JSONDecodeError — feeding the layer-5 permanent-drop path.
findings.recommendation: Pass strict=False everywhere model output is decoded: `json.JSONDecoder(strict=False)` in shared/utils.py:90, and `json.loads(..., strict=False)` at step1_dilemmas.py:564, 578, 584, 600. strict=False only relaxes control characters inside strings, so it cannot admit wrong-shaped data. Add a control-character regression test per parser (copy the pattern from tests/test_dad_steps.py:210-214).

findings.title: Seven divergent parse implementations with three conflicting salvage philosophies; consolidate onto shared/utils.extract_json plus one documented salvage variant
findings.evidence: extract_json (shared/utils.py:68-111) implements longest-complete-value with explicit fragment disqualification ('salvaging such a fragment would feed the caller a wrong-shaped result'). step1_dilemmas.py:571-604 implements the opposite philosophy — _salvage_objects (541-568) deliberately harvests complete objects out of broken arrays. step2_responses.py:37-55 implements a third variant (greedy find('{')..rfind('}') slice, returns {}). audit_sdf.py:363-380 implements a fourth (first-bracket raw_decode, raises). score_sdf.py:61-70 and score_dad.py:92-102 duplicate a fifth inline (fence-strip + bare json.loads with no prose tolerance at all). Five of the six independently reimplement the same fence-stripping lines (`if text.startswith("```"): text = "\n".join(text.split("\n")[1:])`).
findings.failure_scenario: Concrete maintenance cost for the receiving lab: any fix to parsing (the strict=False fix above, a fence edge case, a wrapper-object unwrap) must be discovered and applied in six places, and history shows it isn't — the strict=False lesson was paid for once in step 2 and never propagated, and the '#59 robust-json-extraction' PR hardened only extract_json while the five siblings kept their old bugs. Each new stage a non-engineer contributor adds copies whichever parser they saw last, inheriting its quirks (score_sdf/score_dad copied the weakest one, which cannot even tolerate leading prose, so a judge saying 'Here is my evaluation: {...}' becomes a placeholder-zero record).
findings.recommendation: Consolidation design: (1) extend extract_json with `expect: Literal['array','object'] | None = None` — filter candidates to the expected type before the longest-value rule (this also fixes the '[2] aside' class by construction) — and strict=False; keep the raise-on-broken-container semantics. (2) Move _salvage_objects to shared/utils as `salvage_json_objects(text)` with its docstring stating the contract: fragment-harvesting is safe ONLY where the caller re-requests missing items by id (step 1b is the sole qualifying site). (3) Migrate unchanged: layer1:44, layer2:59, layer5:80 (add expect='array'/'object'); score_sdf.py:61-70 and score_dad.py:92-102 → extract_json(raw, expect='object') in a try/except (strictly more tolerant than today); audit_sdf._parse_json_block → delete, call extract_json (all three callers already catch Exception; first-bracket vs longest-value differences are benign there). (4) Migrate with documented behavior notes: _parse_scope → extract_json(expect='object') wrapped to return {} (greedy-slice → longest-value is a strict improvement; keep _valid_scope); _parse_json_object → extract_json(expect='object') falling back to salvage_json_objects()[0]; _parse_json_array keeps its unique tolerance as extract_json(expect='array') falling back to salvage_json_objects(). (5) Move the fence-stripping into extract_json once (it already handles fences via raw_decode, so the per-site stripping can simply be deleted).
findings.verifier_notes: Read all six cited locations; every line range, mechanism, and quoted docstring phrase checks out: extract_json (utils.py:68-111) refuses fragments, step1's _salvage_objects/_parse_json_array/_parse_json_object (541-604) deliberately harvest them, step2's _parse_scope (37-55) is a greedy slice returning {}, audit_sdf._parse_json_block (363-380) raw_decodes and raises, and score_sdf (61-70)/score_dad (92-102) do bare json.loads that turns any leading prose into a checkpointed placeholder-zero record. Git confirms PR #59 (678dafe) added extract_json and migrated only SDF layers 1/2/5, leaving the five siblings untouched, and strict=False exists only in step2_responses.py — both historical claims hold. Only nit: the fence-strip lines are duplicated at six sibling sites, not "five of the six" (unless the two score-script copies are grouped), which understates rather than overstates the problem.

findings.title: Layer-4 tag-extraction fallback silently ships un-rewritten drafts into the training corpus with no stop_reason check or retry
findings.evidence: Lines 52-61: if `re.search(r"<improved_document>(.*?)</improved_document>", raw, flags=re.DOTALL)` finds no match, the code sets `review_notes = "Parse error — no <improved_document> tags; kept original draft."` and `rewritten = draft["content"]`, then checkpoints the record as done (line 80). The call at lines 43-49 does not request return_stop_reason, and max_tokens=6000 equals layer 3's draft budget, so review-notes + a long rewrite can exceed it. CLAUDE.md's claim 'Every generation call rejects truncated output (stop_reason checked; failed work is not checkpointed)' holds only for DAD steps 2/3 — layers 3/4/5 and DAD 1b/1c never check stop_reason.
findings.failure_scenario: A near-6000-token draft plus the model's review notes exceeds max_tokens; the closing </improved_document> tag never arrives, the regex misses, and the ORIGINAL un-rewritten draft is checkpointed as the 'rewrite'. The doc then only needs to score 7+ at layer 5 to enter the training corpus having silently skipped the pass the code itself calls 'the pipeline's most leverage-heavy call (TCW's ablation: removing it cost 19x on misalignment rate)'. The only trace is a note buried in rewrites.jsonl; nothing aggregates or surfaces the count. Related instance: layer3's untagged fallback (layer3_draft.py:160-164) fuses an entire multi-document response into ONE corpus document instead of dropping it.
findings.recommendation: In layer4, request return_stop_reason=True; on stop_reason=='max_tokens' retry once at a doubled budget (the exact pattern step3_rewrite.py:65-70 already implements), and on a still-missing tag skip without checkpointing so --resume retries, logging to a rewrite_failures.jsonl. findings.title: Eval judges write placeholder-zero scores on parse failure and checkpoint them permanently, silently skewing delivered quality statistics

Coverage report: both files 0% tested.
findings.failure_scenario: A judge model prefixes responses with one sentence of prose for 10% of docs. Those records become permanent zeros; the printed summary the team uses to compare runs ('avg alignment 7.9 → 7.1') reports a phantom quality regression, and the checkpoint guarantees re-running the eval never corrects it. Since these scores are the corpus quality evidence handed to the frontier lab, the delivered numbers are silently wrong in the pessimistic direction.
findings.recommendation: Replace the inline fence-strip + json.loads with utils.extract_json(raw, expect='object') (strictly more tolerant); on parse failure do NOT append or mark_done — print and continue so a rerun retries only the failed docs; and exclude any residual parse-failure records from the aggregate lines (report 'N unparsed' separately). Refactor each script's loop body into a testable run() and add the parse-happy-path / malformed-response / resume tests CLAUDE.md already mandates for every stage.
